newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: G10 bank supervisors to emphasise risk management.
newsitem.headline: G10 bank supervisors to emphasise risk management.

text.p: Group of 10 (G10) bank supervisors will continue to focus on strenthening banks' risk management as well as improving ties with colleagues from emerging countries and the financial sector, the new chairman of the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision said.

Tom de Swaan, who took over as head of the Basle Committee last month, also said supervisors were monitoring efforts by commercial banks to model credit risks -- still the overriding source of losses at banks -- but they would be very cautious before revising the 1988 Basle Capital Accord.

But the main theme that will pervade the Basle Committee's work under de Swaan's leadership will be cooperation -- both on a global scale with non-G10 countries and with supervisors from the insurance and the securities industries.
"Overall there is a cooperative spirit with the non-G10 countries and the Joint Forum," de Swaan, 51, told Reuters in his first interview since taking up his new post.
De Swaan, director of banking supervision at the Dutch central bank, replaced highly-respected Tommaso Padoa-Schioppa, who headed the Basle Committee from 1993 until April this year.

The Basle Committee, based at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) in the Swiss city of Basle, is a forum for cooperation among bank supervisors from G10 leading industrial nations and Luxembourg.

The committee was formed in 1974 and is best known for the 1988 Capital Accord which required international banks to hold capital of eight percent of risk-weighted assets. It has no formal supranational authority, but relies on the moral authority of G10 to pursuade countries to adopt its guidelines.
The Joint Forum on Financial Conglomerates groups supervisors from the three branches of the financial sector. De Swaan currently chairs the forum, but plans to step down.
Capital standards are facing growing criticism for being a crude, one-size-fits-all measure that is no longer an adequate method on which to base supervisory action.

De Swaan said the Basle Committee is closely following the development of new models that more accurately measure credit risks, but he said most of these models -- which he termed as "experiments" -- were still fairly limited.

"Supervisors should be very careful in adopting new methods of assessing credit risk before accepting it as standards of supervision. We follow developments very closely and discuss them in the Basle Committee and that is as far as we are at this moment," de Swaan said.
In recent years the paradigm of banking regulation has shifted toward risk management from capital standards and de Swaan said this evolution would continue.

"More and more we will look at issues of risk management, whereby supervisors should look at the ability to use systems used by financial institutions themselves to asses risk. You set minimum standards as far as how and what risk management should live up to," de Swaan said.
As an example of this shift was a recent committee proposal on how banks should manage interest rate risks.
"I foresee looking at these issues very closely," he said.

Improving the economic health of emerging countries is a top priority for international policy makers and it has become clear that a stable financial system, including a healthy banking sector, is crucial to achieving this goal, de Swaan said.

As part of G10's strategy for improving financial stability in emerging markets, the Basle Committee and banking supervisors from 15 emerging countries in April released 25 Core Principles, the first move toward global standards for banking supervision.

The principles, which de Swaan described as a remarkable achievement from an institutional aspect and for their content, will be used by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and other bodies as a benchmark to measure the effectiveness of supervisory authorities in individual countries, de Swaan said.
De Swaan took issue with a view held by some officials that the Basle Committee had been overly occupied with G10 issues and been slow to tackle the challenges of non-G10 countries.
"I think that in former years attention has also been given to non-G10 countries," de Swaan said.
Not only have past recommendations by the Basle Committee been widely adopted by non-G10 countries, but recent work has been done in cooperation with emerging countries.
"Basically all countries in the world have accepted the 1988 Capital Accord as a minimum standard for capital standards so in that respect it served as worldwide applicable rule," he said.

A recent report on standards for supervising cross-border operations of international banks was written in cooperation between the Basle Committee and the Offshore Group of Banking Supervisors and approved by supervisors from some 140 countries at the Stockholm supervisors' conference in June 1996.
G10 comprises the 11 countries of the United States, Japan, Germany, Canada, Britain, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium, Switzerland and Switzerland.
